solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Go put one pound in hat

indicators.note: to put something in another is to place it inside, so these letters go within the word for go

blocks.note: to have a go is to have a try
the Roman numeral for one
the standard abbreviation for a pound in weight

explanation.surface: An instruction to tuck a pound coin into a hat, perhaps for a busker or a raffle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound' here is the weight abbreviation, not money.
explanation.definitionFit: A trilby is a soft felt hat with an indented crown and narrow brim.

clue.text: In the end you grow fat, gruesome – it’s a test of pulling power

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter
something gruesome is mangled, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the last letter of you
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grim warning that you'll end up fat, set against a test of attraction.
explanation.definitionFit: A tug of war is a contest in which two teams haul on a rope, testing which pulls harder.

clue.text: How time might pass during labour, short of oxygen and confused

indicators.note: being short of an element means missing its symbol, so the letter is removed
confused letters are muddled into a different order

blocks.note: during a period is in it
taken as written; the O, symbol for oxygen, goes

explanation.surface: A woman in childbirth, breathless and disoriented, losing track of the hours.
explanation.walkthrough: IN A BLUR: IN followed by the shuffled letters of LABOUR without its O.
explanation.definitionFit: When hours pass in a blur they rush by so fast that nothing stands out clearly.

clue.text: Tight as an old pair after bar’s opened

indicators.note: a word that is opened shows only its opening letter here

blocks.note: the first letter of bar
an old pair of tights is typically full of runs

explanation.surface: A clue playing on tights, 'Tight' suggesting hosiery, as worn and ruined as an old pair.
explanation.walkthrough: Tight here means drunk, not hosiery; British 'laddered' tights have runs in them, and 'bladdered' is British slang for very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal British terms for being heavily intoxicated after drinking too much alcohol.

clue.text: Former Dutch bank’s part taken over by Luxembourg – that’s odd

indicators.note: something taken over is turned upside down, which in a down-reading sense means read back to front

blocks.note: ABN AMRO was a Dutch bank; this is the first half of its name
the other part of that bank's name
L is the international vehicle code for Luxembourg

explanation.surface: A financial news item about a defunct Dutch bank having a division bought by a Luxembourg firm, and the writer finding it strange.
explanation.walkthrough: The bank's name has two halves; 'part' points to the second one only, and that alone is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Something abnormal departs from the usual pattern, which is exactly what calling a thing odd implies.

clue.text: Basic command of literacy and of conversation each given upper B

blocks.note: a B placed on top, at the start
to read is the core skill of literacy
taken as written
the second B, given to the next word too
to utter words is the basis of conversation

explanation.surface: An educational demand that reading and speaking skills each get a top B grade.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'upper' means placed on top, and 'each' means both words get their own B.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread-and-butter matters are the everyday fundamentals, the most basic and essential part of something.

clue.text: Guts required to kill mafia boss

blocks.note: to off someone is slang for to kill them
Al Capone, the Chicago gangster

explanation.surface: It takes nerve to murder a mob leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guts' looks like courage, but it means entrails.
explanation.definitionFit: Offal is the edible internal organs of an animal, which are its guts.

clue.text: Stupid, middle-of-the-road skating – there’s no end to it

indicators.note: having no end means the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: MOR is the standard abbreviation for middle-of-the-road music
skating takes place on ice; the last letter goes

explanation.surface: A sneering verdict on a bland ice-skating routine that seems to go on forever.
explanation.definitionFit: Moronic describes behaviour typical of a fool, lacking intelligence or good sense.

clue.text: Changing course, fish rises to get room to manoeuvre

indicators.note: in a down clue something that rises is read from the bottom up

blocks.note: a ship yaws when it swings off its course
a snake-like fish

explanation.surface: A fish swerving upward through the water to find space to move.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeway is the margin of freedom or flexibility one has in acting.

clue.text: Bog-standard reshuffle for Mr Cameron? God, no

indicators.note: a reshuffle reorders cabinet posts, so the following letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dismissive reaction to David Cameron's shadow cabinet reshuffle as unremarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2009 David Cameron was leader of the Conservative opposition, so a reshuffle of his team was topical.
explanation.definitionFit: Common-or-garden and bog-standard are both informal British phrases for something entirely ordinary and unremarkable.

clue.text: Leaving road, watchman is abandoning underwear for dip

indicators.note: when the abbreviation for road is leaving, those letters depart from the watchman's word
the little word is is abandoned, so it drops out of the garment's name

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for road, which is removed
a guard keeps watch
taken as written, and removed
a camisole is a light sleeveless undergarment

explanation.surface: A night watchman strips off his underwear and goes for a swim after leaving the road.
explanation.walkthrough: GUARD loses RD to leave GUA; CAMISOLE loses IS to leave CAMOLE; together GUACAMOLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Guacamole is a Mexican avocado-based mixture served for scooping up with crisps or tortilla chips.

clue.text: Absurdity of priest rejecting the church

indicators.note: a priest rejecting a word throws it out, so those letters are removed from his title

blocks.note: Father is the title of a Catholic priest
taken as written, and removed
CE stands for the Church of England

explanation.surface: A clergyman turning his back on the church strikes someone as a nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'the' does double duty: it is both the letters removed from FATHER and part of 'the church'.
explanation.definitionFit: A farce is a ludicrous situation or comic play built on improbable events, hence an absurdity.

clue.text: Recasting of mild mannered lead in the movies

indicators.note: recasting a play reassigns its parts, so the letters are given new positions
the lead of a word is its front, so only its opening letter is used

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of mannered

explanation.surface: A film actor known for gentle, well-mannered roles is replaced in the leading part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mild mannered' reads as one phrase, but it splits: mild is fodder and mannered supplies only its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Filmdom is the world of cinema and those who work in it, the same realm meant by the movies.

clue.text: Lead scrawled around final objects to be excised

indicators.note: a scrawled word is written messily, so its letters come out jumbled
around means wrapping one piece about another, so the jumbled letters surround the word for final

blocks.note: taken as written
the final part of something is its end

explanation.surface: Pencil scribbled round the last items that a censor wants cut out.
explanation.walkthrough: Delenda is Latin for 'things to be deleted', as in Cato's Carthago delenda est.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin gerundive plural names items that must be struck out or destroyed, so they are things to be removed.

clue.text: Broadcaster’s dirty laundry might go here after clean-up

definitions.text: dirty laundry might go here after clean-up

blocks.note: first meaning: one who puts a programme on the air

blocks.clueFragment: dirty laundry might go here after clean-up
blocks.note: second meaning: a frame on which washed clothes are hung to dry

explanation.surface: A TV channel that exposes scandal, then tidies it away afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: To air dirty laundry is to make private scandal public, which is what a broadcaster does; once washed, real laundry goes on a drying rack.
explanation.definitionFit: An airer is both one who airs a show on radio or TV and a household clothes-drying rack.

clue.text: Detainees not starting time in jail, rejecting porridge?

indicators.note: a word not starting has lost its opening letter
in places the preceding letters inside the slang word for jail

blocks.note: cons are convicts, short for convicts; the C is dropped
T is the standard abbreviation for time
nick is British slang for a prison or police station

explanation.surface: Prisoners refusing the prison breakfast, porridge also being British slang for doing time.
explanation.walkthrough: Porridge is also British slang for a jail term, which fits the prison picture; cons are convicts.
explanation.definitionFit: A non-stick pan has a coating that food will not cling to, so it figuratively refuses porridge.

clue.text: Prevention of growth in you-know-what

indicators.note: in sets the first item inside the second

blocks.note: a thing is what you call something you won't name
a small growth on the skin

explanation.surface: A coy reference to stopping a growth on an unmentionable body part.
explanation.definitionFit: Thwarting is the act of blocking or frustrating someone's plans, which amounts to preventing them.

clue.text: Weakness those days being incontinent, spaced out

indicators.note: split with a space, incontinent becomes in continent, so the period goes inside a landmass

blocks.note: the largest continent
those days are back then

explanation.surface: An old person's frailty, having become incontinent and confused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spaced out' looks like part of the picture, but tells you to read incontinent as two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Asthenia is the medical term for abnormal physical feebleness or loss of strength.

clue.text: Building society shortly bringing back bar on property seizure

indicators.note: bringing a word back means running it in the opposite direction

blocks.note: the short form L and G, for Legal and General
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mortgage lender briefly placing a ban on someone's house.
explanation.walkthrough: L&G is Legal and General, a large British insurer rather than a building society; the setter owned up to that slip on the blog.
explanation.definitionFit: A land grab is the sudden, often unlawful, taking of territory or real estate.

clue.text: Pneumatic mover shows off curvy bit

blocks.note: to air something is to show it off
the hip is a curvy part of the body

explanation.surface: A shapely woman flaunting her curves, pneumatic being slang for buxom.
explanation.walkthrough: Pneumatic is old slang for a full-figured woman, but here it means air-filled.
explanation.definitionFit: An airship is a gas-filled aircraft, so it is literally a vehicle borne along by air.

clue.text: Non-drinker was consuming more than one unit

indicators.note: consuming means taking something inside, so the abstainer goes within the other word

blocks.note: taken as written
TT means teetotal

explanation.surface: A teetotaller who nonetheless downed several units of alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unit' suggests alcohol units, but it is the unit of electrical power.
explanation.definitionFit: The watt is the SI unit of power, so the plural names several of those measures.

clue.text: Teaching union getting into difficulty about independent head

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
letters in difficulty are in a mess, so they are jumbled
about means going round, so the jumbled letters enclose the single letter

blocks.note: TU stands for trade union
taken as written
the first letter of independent

explanation.surface: A teachers' union in trouble over the school's independent head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Into' looks like a link between union and difficulty, but it is the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuition is instruction given to a pupil, especially privately, which is teaching.

clue.text: To make up for Australia’s victory over England – twice…

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for Australia
V for victory
the usual abbreviation
England again, by its one-letter abbreviation

explanation.surface: Australia winning against England in a sporting rivalry such as the Ashes, again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' places V before ENG; 'twice' means England is clued a second time, as E. The ellipsis runs on to the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To avenge a wrong is to exact retribution for it, settling the score and so compensating for it.

clue.text: Woman gathering mountain plant

indicators.note: gathering means drawing something in, so the woman's name holds the next word

blocks.note: a woman's name
ben is a Scottish word for mountain, as in Ben Nevis

explanation.surface: A woman picking wild flowers on a mountainside.
explanation.definitionFit: Verbena is a genus of garden and wild flowering herbs, also called vervain.

clue.text: … England would triumph with this fellow

blocks.note: E is an abbreviation for England
the 'd of I'd, short for would
to triumph is to win

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: England's hope of revenge rests on this one player.
explanation.definitionFit: Edwin is a man's name, so it can stand for a fellow the clue points to.

clue.text: Like mere soil?

blocks.note: a mere and a tarn are both small lakes
the suffix -ish means like or resembling

explanation.surface: A question asking whether something resembles ordinary dirt.
explanation.walkthrough: Mere looks like 'only', but it is the lake; the suffix comes after it even though 'Like' is printed first.
explanation.definitionFit: To tarnish is to dull or stain a surface, much as to soil it is to make it dirty.

clue.text: Not at all disrespectful term for woman in this day and age

indicators.note: in places the slang term inside the phrase for the present

blocks.note: this day and age is the present
a slang, derogatory word for a woman

explanation.surface: A firm refusal to tolerate demeaning words for women nowadays.
explanation.definitionFit: Nohow is a dialect or informal adverb meaning in no way whatsoever.

clue.text: Dreadful artist in broadcast who tells you what to eat

definitions.text: who tells you what to eat

indicators.note: something broadcast is heard, so it is the sound of the phrase that counts

blocks.note: dire is dreadful and Titian the Venetian painter

explanation.surface: A poor painter shows up on television.
explanation.definitionFit: A dietitian is a health professional advising people on nutrition and what food they should consume.

clue.text: One setting forth from river northeast not leaving Ohio

indicators.note: the abbreviation for the US state leaves, so its letter is taken out of the word

blocks.note: ex is Latin for from
the Po is Italy's longest river
NE is the compass abbreviation
taken as written; the O goes

explanation.surface: Someone travelling out from a river region to the north-east, though not heading out of Ohio.
explanation.walkthrough: O is the abbreviation for Ohio, so NOT loses an O.
explanation.definitionFit: An exponent is one who expounds or sets out an idea or argument for others.

clue.text: Programme had negative contents retracted

indicators.note: contents are what lies inside, so the letters are found within the words
retracted means drawn back, so the found letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: the letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A TV show that withdrew some unfavourable material.
explanation.definitionFit: An agenda is a list or programme of items to be dealt with, as at a meeting.
